definition: To push someone into doing something by using threats or unfair pressure.
example: No tenant should be coerced into signing a lease they have not had time to read.
nuance: To coerce is to get your way through pressure or threats, while to coax is to win someone over gently with charm or rewards.
prompt: A manager wants employees to work over the weekend without extra pay.
options: The manager tried to coerce the staff by hinting that anyone who refused might lose shifts.
The manager tried to coerce the staff by politely asking for volunteers and accepting every no.
The manager hoped to coerce the team with warm pastries and a cheerful thank-you note.
Slowly, the scattered weekend schedules began to coerce into one tidy plan.
reasons: Implying a penalty for saying no is exactly the kind of pressure that forces compliance.
If refusing carries no cost and is freely accepted, nobody is being pressured.
Treats and kindness are ways to coax; the word requires threats or pressure, not charm.
This confuses the word with cohere or coalesce; it needs a person being pushed, not parts joining.

practice.prompt: A student wants to copy a classmate's finished homework.
options: The two students agreed to coerce on the assignment, splitting the problems evenly.
Maya offered to coerce Leo by tutoring him in chemistry if he lent her the pages.
Maya tried to coerce Leo by warning she would spread a rumor about him unless he shared.
Maya tried to coerce Leo by asking once, then shrugging when he shook his head.
reasons: Working together by choice is cooperation; the word means one side compels the other.
A fair trade he can freely decline is a bargain, not a threat or unfair pressure.
Using a threat to make him hand over his work is a clear case of forcing his hand.
A single request dropped at the first refusal involves no pressure at all.
